abstract: Living tissues are active materials whose collective states depend on mechanochemical communication across connected cells. Yet tissues undergoing repair, ageing or tumorigenesis often contain intermingled cells with divergent states. How such heterogeneity alters tissue-scale communication, and whether cell competition can restore it, remains unclear. Here we track ERK activity, a dynamic readout and regulator of epithelial mechanochemical coupling, to ask how tissues recover from an aberrant state containing DNA-damaged cells. We show that damaged cells function as insulators, disrupting long-range ERK waves and partitioning control cells into disconnected clusters. As damaged cells are progressively eliminated by neighbouring control cells, fragmented clusters coalesce into a tissue-scale connected network through a percolation transition. Crossing this topological threshold restores collective ERK waves and coordinated cell motion, indicating recovery of tissue-scale mechanochemical order. Percolation also reshapes competitive elimination: before connectivity is restored, control cells remove damaged neighbours through actin-rich invasive protrusions; after percolation, connected control cells eliminate residual damaged cells by ERK-associated multicellular squeezing. Thus, cell competition actively reconfigures tissue topology to restore collective mechanochemical order.
